sandhi.type: visarga sandhi (special rule for सः), then vowel sandhi
sandhi.rule: एतत्तदोः सुलोपोऽकोरनञ्समासे हलि (6.1.132); अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः (6.1.101)
sandhi.note: The visarga of सः is dropped before the consonant t; तदा + अभिहतः gives ā; अभिहतः before the voiced bh becomes अभिहतो (हशि च, 6.1.114).

morph.note: Perfect of अभि + √हन्: the reduplicated syllable is ज (h → j), and the root’s h becomes gh after it (ज-घान); vṛddhi of the root vowel in the 3rd singular.
Perfect of नि + √पत्: reduplication प-पात with vṛddhi. ‘Fell down’.
Past participle of √मूर्च्छ् ‘to faint, lose consciousness’: Śumbha is stunned, not killed. He returns in chapter 10.

mantras.anvaya: ततः क्रुद्धा सा चण्डिका शूलेन तम् अभिजघान। तदा अभिहतः सः मूर्च्छितः (सन्) भूमौ निपपात ह।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: the blow (subject चण्डिका, instrument शूलेन, object तम्, verb अभिजघान) and its result (subject सः with the participles अभिहतः and मूर्च्छितः, verb निपपात).
mantras.lit: Then that Caṇḍikā, enraged, struck him with her spear. Struck then, he fell senseless on the ground.
mantras.tr: Then Caṇḍikā in her anger struck him with her spear, and Śumbha, struck down, fell senseless to the earth.

comm.t: Śumbha is struck down and swoons. The verse says मूर्च्छितः, ‘fainted’: he is out of the fight for now, which is why Niśumbha, who had himself been felled in 9.16, rises again in the next verse.
The narrative is careful with the two brothers: Niśumbha’s death comes first, in this chapter; Śumbha’s is kept for chapter 10, after the Goddess has drawn all her Śaktis back into herself.

samasa.literal: he by whom a bow has been taken

morph.note: आत्त is the past participle of आ + √दा ‘to take’: after a prefix ending in a vowel, दा’s participle may take the short form -त्त (आत्त, ‘taken’) instead of दत्त.
Absolutive of सम् + प्र + √आप् with ल्यप् (-य), the form used after prefixes: ‘having (re)gained’.
Perfect of आ + √हन्, formed like अभिजघान in 9.28 (ज-घान).

mantras.anvaya: ततः निशुम्भः चेतनां सम्प्राप्य आत्तकार्मुकः (सन्) देवीं कालीं तथा केसरिणं शरैः आजघान।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject (निशुम्भः) with an absolutive phrase (चेतनां सम्प्राप्य) and an epithet (आत्तकार्मुकः); verb आजघान with three objects and the instrument शरैः.
mantras.lit: Then Niśumbha, having regained consciousness, bow taken up, struck with arrows the Goddess, Kālī and the lion as well.
mantras.tr: Then Niśumbha came to his senses, seized his bow, and shot his arrows at the Goddess, at Kālī, and at the lion.

comm.t: Niśumbha, felled by the Goddess’s arrows in 9.16, recovers and returns to the fight while his brother lies stunned. He aims at all three: the Goddess, Kālī and the lion.
The lion is named here by an epithet, केसरिन् ‘the maned one’. It fights throughout as a warrior in its own right (9.21, 9.37).

sandhi.note: The m of बाहूनाम् stays before a vowel; the m of अयुतम् becomes anusvāra before the d of दनुजेश्वरः.
Visarga before ch becomes s, then palatal ś: -aḥ ch- → -aśch-.

samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (दनुज, ‘born of Danu’, is itself an upapada tatpuruṣa: दनोः जातः)
samasa.literal: lord of the sons of Danu
samasa.sense: Niśumbha, a lord of the Dānavas

samasa.type: karmadhāraya (avadhāraṇa: ‘the weapon that is the discus’)
samasa.sense: with a storm of discuses — 9.31 shows there were many (तानि चक्राणि)

morph.note: Periphrastic perfect: the causative/curādi stem छादय- takes -आम् and the perfect of √अस् (आस): छादयाम् + आस. Stems of more than one syllable form their perfect this way.
Absolutive of √कृ with क्त्वा (no prefix, so not ल्यप्). With अयुतं बाहूनाम् it means ‘having made (for himself) ten thousand arms’ — Niśumbha multiplies his body.

mantras.anvaya: पुनः च दनुजेश्वरः दितिजः बाहूनाम् अयुतं कृत्वा चक्रायुधेन चण्डिकां छादयामास।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject (दनुजेश्वरः, with the apposition दितिजः), an absolutive phrase (बाहूनाम् अयुतं कृत्वा), instrument (चक्रायुधेन), verb and object (छादयामास चण्डिकाम्).
mantras.lit: And again the lord of the Dānavas, the son of Diti, having made ten thousand arms, covered Caṇḍikā with discus-weapons.
mantras.tr: Again the Dānava lord took on ten thousand arms, and the son of Diti buried Caṇḍikā under a hail of discuses.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Took on’ renders कृत्वा, ‘having made’; ‘a hail of’ renders the collective singular चक्रायुधेन.

comm.t: Niśumbha’s second assault: he multiplies his arms to ten thousand and hurls discuses from all of them at once. Śumbha had shown eight arms in 9.18; the brothers’ powers of self-multiplication answer the Goddess’s many arms.
दनुज (son of Danu) and दितिज (son of Diti) are used interchangeably of the asuras in the text; both name Niśumbha here.

samasa.vigraha: दुर्गेषु आर्तिः दुर्गार्तिः; दुर्गार्तिं नाशयति इति
samasa.type: upapada tatpuruṣa (with the agent suffix -इन्, fem. -इनी) containing a saptamī tatpuruṣa (दुर्गार्ति)
samasa.literal: she who destroys distress in difficult places
samasa.sense: who ends the suffering of those in hard straits — a play on the name Durgā
samasa.alt: दुर्गार्ति may also be read as a karmadhāraya, दुर्गा (दुःसहा) आर्तिः ‘distress hard to bear’; the sense, deliverance from affliction, is the same.

morph.note: नाशिनी is the feminine of नाशिन्, from the causative of √नश् (नाशय- ‘to destroy’) with the agent suffix -इन्: ‘who habitually destroys’.

mantras.anvaya: ततः क्रुद्धा भगवती दुर्गार्तिनाशिनी दुर्गा स्वशरैः तानि चक्राणि तान् सायकान् च चिच्छेद।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject दुर्गा with three epithets; verb चिच्छेद with two objects (तानि चक्राणि, सायकान् तान्) joined by च, and the instrument स्वशरैः.
mantras.lit: Then the Blessed One, enraged — Durgā, destroyer of distress in hard straits — cut with her own arrows those discuses and those arrows.
mantras.tr: Then the blessed Durgā, who ends all distress in hard places, in her anger cut those discuses to pieces with her arrows, and his arrows too.

comm.t: The ten thousand discuses are cut down as easily as single arrows were. The Goddess is named here Durgā with an epithet that explains the name: she destroys the distress (आर्ति) of the hard place (दुर्ग).

The text tells the origin of the name Durgā in her own prophecy (11.49–50, the slaying of the asura Durgama); here the name is glossed by its other traditional sense, the one who rescues from difficulty.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the name दुर्गा (190), followed directly by दुःखहन्त्री (191), ‘destroyer of sorrow’ — the same pairing of name and gloss as in this verse.

samasa.type: tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa containing a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (दैत्यसेना)
samasa.literal: surrounded by the army of the daityas
samasa.sense: at the head of his host

morph.note: Imperfect of अभि + √धाव्, with the augment अ- after the prefix (अभि + अ + धावत → अभ्यधावत). √धाव् takes both padas: 9.6 has the parasmaipada अभ्यधावत्, this verse the ātmanepada अभ्यधावत.
Absolutive of आ + √दा: with आ the root means ‘to take’, and the ल्यप् absolutive is आदाय, ‘having taken’.
Infinitive of √हन् with तुमुन्, expressing purpose with a verb of motion: ‘rushed … to kill’.

mantras.anvaya: ततः दैत्यसेनासमावृतः निशुम्भः गदाम् आदाय चण्डिकां हन्तुं वै वेगेन अभ्यधावत।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject (निशुम्भः with दैत्यसेनासमावृतः), an absolutive phrase (गदाम् आदाय), a purpose infinitive with its object (चण्डिकां हन्तुम्), manner (वेगेन) and verb (अभ्यधावत).
mantras.lit: Then Niśumbha, surrounded by the army of the daityas, taking up a mace, indeed rushed swiftly to kill Caṇḍikā.
mantras.tr: Then Niśumbha seized a mace and, with the daitya army all around him, charged at Caṇḍikā to kill her.

comm.t: Niśumbha’s third assault: having lost his bow-and-discus attack, he takes a mace and charges in person with his army about him.
Niśumbha had already thrown a mace at the Goddess in 9.15, and her trident burnt it to ash. Each weapon he takes up is answered and undone; this time she will not wait for it to be thrown.
